cues.en: Hi.
cues.zh: 嗨。

cues.en: What is technology? Don't skip ahead. I promise I'm going somewhere with this. So you could have some kind of definition from a dictionary that's like technology is machinery and equipment made using scientific knowledge, something like that. But where are the boundaries of the category? What counts?
cues.zh: 什么是技术？先别急着往下看。我保证这和后面有关。你可能会找到某种字典定义，比如技术是用科学知识制造出来的机械和设备之类。但这个类别的边界在哪里？什么才算？

cues.en: For example, pair of scissors.
cues.zh: 比如一把剪刀。

cues.en: Technology?
cues.zh: 算技术吗？

cues.en: I think most people would say no, although it does meet the definition. Perhaps this is used to be technology, But now I think they're too simple. They're too well understood.
cues.zh: 我想大多数人会说不是，尽管它确实符合定义。也许它曾经算是技术，但现在我觉得它们太简单了。它们太容易理解了。

cues.en: I think once we've really nailed something down and figured out all of the details, people stop thinking of it as technology. I think in order to be technology,
cues.zh: 我觉得，一旦我们把某样东西彻底弄清楚、搞明白所有细节，人们就不再把它当成技术了。我认为要成为技术，

cues.en: something has to be complex and unpredictable.
cues.zh: 某样东西必须复杂且难以预测。

cues.en: Maybe even unreliable. YouTube for example is definitely technology as is the device you're watching this on. Okay. Why does this matter? I guess part of my point is exact definitions are really difficult
cues.zh: 甚至可能不可靠。比如 YouTube 绝对是技术，你正在看这个的设备也是。好。这为什么重要？我想我的部分观点是，准确定义真的很难

cues.en: and this generally isn't much of a problem because language doesn't really work by exact definitions. Maybe it's hard to specify exactly what we mean when we use a word like technology,
cues.zh: 而且这通常不算什么问题，因为语言并不是真的靠精确定义来运作。也许很难准确说明我们用“技术”这样的词时到底指什么，

cues.en: but to paraphrase something from the US Supreme Court, you know it when you see it and that's good enough for most uses. The reason I bring this up is sometimes people ask me about my definition of artificial intelligence
cues.zh: 但套用美国最高法院的一句话来说，你看到它时就知道它，而对大多数用途来说这就够了。我提这个是因为有时人们会问我的人工智能定义

cues.en: and actually think that's pretty similar. You could say that AI is about trying to get machines to carry out human cognitive tasks,
cues.zh: 而且实际上我觉得这很相似。可以说，AI 就是试图让机器执行人类的认知任务，

cues.en: but then arithmetic is a cognitive task. Does that make a calculator artificial intelligence?
cues.zh: 但算术也是一种认知任务。那计算器算人工智能吗？

cues.en: You know, sorting a list is a cognitive task. I don't think most people would call that AI. Playing a perfect game of noughts and crosses used to be considered AI, but I don't think we'd call it that these days. So to me, AI is about making machines do cognitive tasks that we didn't think they could do. Maybe it's because it's about making machines do human cognitive tasks and once machines can do something we no longer think of it as a human cognitive task.
cues.zh: 你知道，给列表排序也是一种认知任务。我不觉得大多数人会把这叫作 AI。过去，完美地下一局井字棋会被视为 AI，但如今我不觉得我们还会这么叫。所以在我看来，AI 是让机器完成那些我们原以为它们做不到的认知任务。也许是因为，AI 本是让机器完成人类的认知任务，而一旦机器能做到某件事，我们就不再把它看作人类的认知任务了。

cues.en: This means that the goalposts are always moving for artificial intelligence. Some people have complained about that but I think it's pretty reasonable to have that as part of the definition.
cues.zh: 这意味着，对人工智能来说，目标门槛总在变化。有人对此抱怨过，但我觉得把这作为定义的一部分挺合理。

cues.en: So that means that the goal of AI research is to continue to expand the range of tasks computers can handle so they can keep surprising us. It used to be that AI research was all about figuring out and formalizing things so that we could write programs to do them.
cues.zh: 所以这意味着，AI 研究的目标是不断扩展计算机能处理的任务范围，让它们继续给我们带来惊喜。过去，AI 研究主要是搞清楚并形式化各种问题，好让我们能编写程序来完成它们。

cues.en: Things like arithmetic,
cues.zh: 比如算术，

cues.en: sorting lists, and playing noughts and crosses, these are all in the class of problems that you might call things we can specify well enough to write programs that do them. And for a long time that was all that we could do. That was the only type of problem we could tackle. But for a lot of problems that approach is really really hard.
cues.zh: 给列表排序、下井字棋，这些都属于一类问题：我们可以把需求描述得足够清楚，从而写出程序来完成。很长一段时间里，我们能做的就只有这些。那是我们唯一能处理的问题类型。但对很多问题来说，这种方法真的真的很难。

cues.en: Like consider, how would you write a program that takes an image of a handwritten digit and determines what digit it is? You can formalize the process and try to write a program. It's actually kind of a fun exercise if you want to get to grips with the old school like computer vision and image processing techniques. And once you've written that program, you can test it using the MNIST dataset
cues.zh: 比如想想，你会怎么写一个程序，输入一张手写数字的图片，判断它是哪个数字？你可以把过程形式化，然后试着写程序。如果你想掌握老派的计算机视觉和图像处理技术，这其实是个挺有趣的练习。而一旦你写好这个程序，就可以用 MNIST 数据集来测试它。

cues.en: which is a giant collection of correctly labeled small images of digits. What you'll find is if you do well then this thing will kind of work but even the best programs written this way don't work that well. They're not really reliable enough to actually use. Someone is always gonna come along with a really blunt pencil and ruin your programs accuracy. And this is still a pretty easy problem. I mean, if you wanted to do something like, letters as well as numbers.
cues.zh: 这是一个庞大的、带正确标注的数字小图像集合。你会发现，如果做得好，这套东西勉强能跑，但即使用这种方式写出的最好的程序，效果也没那么好。它们不够可靠，实际上没法真正使用。总会有人拿着一支很钝的铅笔来捣乱，毁掉你程序的准确率。而且这仍然是个相当简单的问题。我是说，如果你想做类似字母和数字都识别这种事情。

cues.en: Now you have to differentiate between o and zero and one and I and lowercase l.
cues.zh: 现在你得区分字母 o 和数字零、数字一和字母 I，还有小写字母 l。

cues.en: Forget about it. It's never gonna work. And even that is a relatively simple problem. What if you're trying to do something like differentiating
cues.zh: 算了吧，这根本行不通。而且这还是个相对简单的问题。如果你想做的是区分

cues.en: pictures of cats from pictures of dogs?
cues.zh: 猫的图片和狗的图片呢？

cues.en: This whole approach is just not gonna work for that. But there is a fact that we can exploit which is that it's a lot easier to evaluate a solution than to generate a solution for a lot of these problems. I've talked about this before. I couldn't generate a good rocket design myself but I can tell you that this one
cues.zh: 这套方法对那个完全行不通。但有个事实可以利用：对很多这类问题，评估一个解比生成一个解容易得多。我之前谈过这个。我自己设计不出好的火箭，但我能告诉你，这一版

cues.en: needs work.
cues.zh: 还得改进。

cues.en: It's easier to write a program to evaluate an output than to write one to produce that output. So maybe it's too hard to write a program that performs the task of identifying handwritten numbers, but it's pretty easy to write a program that evaluates how well a given program does at that task. As long as you have a load of correctly labeled examples.
cues.zh: 写程序来评估一个输出，比写程序来产生这个输出更容易。所以，写一个识别手写数字的程序也许太难，但写一个评估某个程序在这项任务上表现如何的程序却相当容易，只要你有大量正确标注的样本。

cues.en: You just keep giving it labeled examples from the dataset and you see how many it gets right. In the same way, maybe you can't write a program that plays an Atari game well, but you can easily write a program that tells you how well you're doing. You just read off the score. And this is where machine learning comes in. It gives you ways to take a program for evaluating solutions
cues.zh: 你只需不断给它数据集里带标签的样本，然后看它答对了多少。同样，也许你写不出一个能玩好 Atari 游戏的程序，但你可以轻松写一个程序来告诉你自己表现得多好。你只要读出分数就行。这就是机器学习的用武之地。它提供了一些方法，让你能利用一个评估解的程序。

cues.en: and use it to create good solutions.
cues.zh: 并用它来构建好的解决方案。

cues.en: All you need is a dataset with a load of labeled examples or a game with a score or some other way of programmatically evaluating the outputs, and you can train a system that carries out the task. There's a sense in which this is a new programming paradigm.
cues.zh: 你只需要一个包含大量标注样本的数据集，或者一个带评分的游戏，或者某种能以编程方式评估输出的方法，就能训练出一个执行该任务的系统。某种意义上，这是一种新的编程范式。

cues.en: Instead of writing the program itself,
cues.zh: 而不是直接编写程序本身，

cues.en: you write the reward function or the loss function or whatever, and the training process finds you a set of parameters for your network that perform well according to that function. If you squint, the training process is sort of like a compiler.
cues.zh: 你编写奖励函数、损失函数或其他类似的东西，训练过程会为你的网络找到一组在该函数下表现良好的参数。粗略一看，训练过程有点像编译器。

cues.en: It's taking code you've written and turning it into an executable that actually performs the task. So in this way, machine learning expands the class of tasks that machines can start to perform. It's no longer just tasks that you can write programs to do, but tasks that you can write programs to evaluate. But if this is a form of programming, it's a very difficult one. Anyone who has programmed in c or c plus plus will tell you that the two scariest words you can see in a specification are undefined
cues.zh: 它是把你写的代码变成一个真正能执行任务的可执行程序。所以这样一来，机器学习扩展了机器能够执行的任务类别。不再只是你能写程序去做的任务，而是你能写程序去评估的任务。但如果这是一种编程形式，那它也是非常困难的一种。任何用 C 或 C++ 编程过的人都会告诉你，在规范里能看到的最吓人的两个词就是“未定义”

cues.en: behavior. So how many folks here are little bit afraid of undefined behavior in their source code? Everybody. And machine learning as a programming paradigm is pretty much entirely undefined behavior.
cues.zh: 行为。那么这里有多少人有点害怕自己源代码里的未定义行为？所有人。而机器学习作为一种编程范式，几乎完全就是未定义行为。

cues.en: And as a consequence, programs created in this way tend to have a lot of quite serious bugs. These And are things that I've talked about before on the channel. For example, reward gaming
cues.zh: 因此，用这种方式创建的程序往往会有很多相当严重的 bug。这些也是我在频道里之前讲过的问题。比如奖励钻空子，

cues.en: where there's some subtle difference between the reward function you wrote and the actual reward function that you kind of meant to write and an agent will find ways to exploit that difference to get high reward, to find things it can do which the reward function you wrote gives a high reward to but the reward function you meant to write wouldn't have. Or the problem of side effects where you aren't able to specify in the reward function everything that you care about and the agent will assume that anything not mentioned in the reward function is of zero value which can lead to it having large negative side effects. There are a bunch more of these specification problems
cues.zh: 也就是你写的奖励函数和你真正想写的奖励函数之间存在一些细微差别，而智能体会想方设法利用这种差别来获得高奖励，找到一些它能做的事——你写的奖励函数会给高奖励，但你真正想写的奖励函数不会。还有副作用问题：你无法在奖励函数中指定所有你关心的东西，而智能体会认为奖励函数中未提及的任何东西价值都为零，这可能导致它产生巨大的负面副作用。这类规范问题还有很多。

cues.en: and in general this way of creating programs is a safety nightmare, but also it still doesn't allow machines to do all of the tasks that we might want them to do. A lot of tasks are just too complex and too poorly defined to write good evaluation functions for. For example, if you have a robot and you want it to scramble you an egg, how do you write a function which takes input from the robot senses and returns how well the robot is doing it scrambling an egg. That's a very difficult problem. Even something simple like getting a simulated robot to do a backflip is actually pretty hard to specify.
cues.zh: 总的来说，这种创建程序的方式是安全噩梦，而且它仍然无法让机器完成我们可能希望它们完成的所有任务。很多任务太复杂、定义太差，很难写出好的评估函数。比如，你有一个机器人，想让它给你炒个鸡蛋，你怎么写一个函数，接收机器人传感器的输入，并返回它炒鸡蛋做得有多好？这是个非常困难的问题。甚至像让模拟机器人做后空翻这样简单的事，实际上也很难明确指定。

cues.en: What we do about this? Well, normal reinforcement learning looks like this.
cues.zh: 那怎么解决呢？普通的强化学习是这样的。

cues.en: You have an agent and an environment. The agent takes actions in the environment and the environment produces observations and rewards.
cues.zh: 你有一个智能体和一个环境。智能体在环境中采取行动，环境产生观测和奖励。

cues.en: The rewards are calculated by the reward function. That's where you program in what you want the agent to do. So some researchers tried this with the backflip task. They spent a couple of hours writing a reward function and it looks like this and the result of training the agent with this reward function looks like this.
cues.zh: 奖励由奖励函数计算。你就是在奖励函数里编写希望智能体做什么。于是有些研究者用后空翻任务试了试。他们花了几个小时写奖励函数，看起来像这样，而用这个奖励函数训练智能体的结果看起来像这样。

cues.en: I guess it's that's basically a backflip.
cues.zh: 我猜这基本上就是后空翻吧。

cues.en: I've seen better. Something like evaluating a backflip is very hard to specify
cues.zh: 我见过更好的。像评判后空翻这种事，很难明确说明

cues.en: but it's not actually hard to do. Like it's easy to tell if something is doing a backflip just by looking at it. It's just hard to write a program that does that. So what if you just directly put yourself in there, if you just play the part of the reward function?
cues.zh: 但实际做起来并不难。就像只要看一眼，就很容易判断某个东西是不是在后空翻。难的是写出能做这件事的程序。那如果你直接把自己放进去，如果你来扮演奖励函数呢？

cues.en: Every time step you look at the state and you give the agent a number for how well you think it's doing at backflipping. People have tried that kind of approach but it has a bunch of problems. The main one is these systems generally need to spend huge amounts of time interacting with the environment in order to learn even simple things. So you're gonna be sitting there saying, no, that's not a backflip.
cues.zh: 每个时间步，你观察状态，然后给智能体一个数值，表示你认为它后空翻做得多好。人们试过这类方法，但它有一堆问题。主要问题是，这些系统通常需要花大量时间与环境交互，才能学会哪怕很简单的事情。所以你会坐在那儿说，不对，那不是后空翻。

cues.en: No, that's not a backflip either.
cues.zh: 不，那也不是后空翻。

cues.en: That was closer.
cues.zh: 这次更接近了。

cues.en: Nope, that's worse again. And you're gonna do this for hundreds of hours.
cues.zh: 不行，这次又更差了。而且你得这样练上几百个小时。

cues.en: Nobody has time for that. So what can we do?
cues.zh: 没人有那么多时间。那我们能怎么办？

cues.en: Well, you may notice that this problem is a little bit like identifying handwritten digits, isn't it? We can't figure out how to write a program to do it and it's too time consuming to do it ourselves.
cues.zh: 你可能会注意到，这个问题有点像识别手写数字，对吧？我们想不出怎么写程序来完成它，而自己动手做又太耗时。

cues.en: So why not take the approach that people take with handwritten numbers?
cues.zh: 那为什么不采用人们处理手写数字时用的方法呢？

cues.en: Why not learn a reward function? But it's not quite as simple as it sounds. Backflips are harder than handwritten digits in part because where are you gonna get your data from? For digits, we have this dataset MNIST. We have this giant collection of correctly labeled images. We built that by having humans write lots of numbers, scanning them, and then labeling the images. We need humans to do the thing, to provide examples to learn from. We need demonstrations.
cues.zh: 为什么不学习一个奖励函数？但事情并没有听起来那么简单。后空翻比手写数字更难，部分原因在于：你从哪里获得数据？对于数字，我们有 MNIST 数据集。我们有一大批正确标注的图像。我们让人写大量数字、扫描它们，然后给图像打标签，才构建出这个数据集。我们需要人类去做这件事，提供可供学习的示例。我们需要示范。

cues.en: Now if you have good demonstrations of an agent performing a task, can do things like imitation learning and inverse reinforcement learning which are pretty cool but they're a subject for a later video. But with backflips we don't have that. I'm not even sure if I can do a backflip and that wouldn't help anyway. Wait, really?
cues.zh: 现在，如果你有智能体执行任务的良好示范，就可以做模仿学习和逆强化学习之类的事，这很酷，但那是之后视频的主题。但后空翻我们没有这种示范。我甚至不确定自己能不能做后空翻，而且就算能也没用。等等，真的吗？

cues.en: No, don't have to do it. No, we don't need a recording of a human backflipping. We
cues.zh: 不，不用做。不，我们不需要人类后空翻的录像。我们

cues.zh: 需要的是这个机器人后空翻的录像，对吧？它们的生理结构不一样。

cues.en: But I don't think I could puppeteer the simulated robot to backflip either. That would be like playing co op on nightmare mode. So we can't demonstrate the task. So what do we do? Well, we go back to the Supreme Court. Exactly defining a back flip is hard, doing a back flip is hard, but I know a back flip when I see one.
cues.zh: 但我觉得我也没法操控模拟机器人做后空翻。那就像在噩梦模式下玩合作游戏。所以我们没法演示这个任务。那怎么办？我们回到最高法院。精确定义后空翻很难，做后空翻也很难，但我看到后空翻就能认出来。

cues.en: So we need a setup that learns a good reward function without demonstrations,
cues.zh: 所以我们需要一个无需演示就能学习良好奖励函数的方案，

cues.en: just by using human feedback,
cues.zh: 仅通过使用人类反馈，

cues.en: without requiring too much of the humans time. And that's what this paper does. It's called deep reinforcement learning from human preferences and it's actually a collaboration between OpenAI and DeepMind. The paper documents a system that works by reward modeling. If you give it an hour of feedback,
cues.zh: 而不需要占用人类太多时间。这就是这篇论文所做的。它叫基于人类偏好的深度强化学习，实际上是 OpenAI 和 DeepMind 的合作。论文记录了一个通过奖励建模工作的系统。如果你给它一小时的反馈，

cues.en: it does this.
cues.zh: 它就是这样做的。

cues.en: That looks a lot better than two hours of reward function writing. So how does reward modeling work? Well, let's go back to the diagram. In reward modeling, instead of the human writing the reward function or just being the reward function,
cues.zh: 这看起来比花两个小时写奖励函数好多了。那么奖励建模是怎么工作的呢？好，我们回到那张图。在奖励建模中，不是由人来编写奖励函数，或者干脆让人本身充当奖励函数，

cues.en: we instead replace the reward function with a reward model implemented as a neural network. So the agent interacts with the environment in the normal way except the rewards it's getting are coming from the reward model. The reward model behaves just like a regular reward function in that it gets observations from the environment and gives rewards. But the way it decides those rewards is with a neural network which is trying to predict what reward a human would give. Okay. How does the reward model learn what reward a human would give? Well, the human provides it with feedback.
cues.zh: 而是用一个以神经网络实现的奖励模型来替代奖励函数。于是，智能体以正常方式与环境交互，只不过它得到的奖励来自奖励模型。奖励模型的行为就像一个常规奖励函数：它从环境获取观测并给出奖励。但它决定这些奖励的方式，是通过一个神经网络来预测人类会给出什么奖励。好。奖励模型如何学习人类会给出什么奖励呢？嗯，人类会向它提供反馈。

cues.en: So the way that works is the agent is interacting with the environment, know trying to learn and then the system will extract
cues.zh: 所以它的工作方式是，智能体与环境交互，试图学习，然后系统会提取

cues.en: two short clips of the agent flailing about just a second or two and it presents those two clips to the human and the human decides which they like better, which one is more back flippy and the reward model then uses that feedback in basically the standard supervised learning way. It tries to find a reward function such that in situations where the human prefers the left clip to the right clip, the reward function gives more reward to the agent in the left clip than the right clip and vice versa.
cues.zh: 智能体胡乱扑腾一两秒的两段短片段，把这两段片段展示给人类，由人类决定更喜欢哪段、哪段后空翻更多，奖励模型随后基本按标准监督学习的方式利用这些反馈。它试图找到一个奖励函数，使得在人类更偏好左边片段而非右边片段的情况下，奖励函数给左边片段中智能体的奖励高于右边片段，反之亦然。

cues.en: So which clip gets more reward from the reward model ends up being a good predictor of which clip the human will prefer,
cues.zh: 所以，哪个片段从奖励模型那里获得更多奖励，最终能很好地预测人类会更偏好哪个片段，

cues.en: which should mean that the reward model ends up being very similar to the reward function the human really wants. But the thing I like about this is the whole thing is happening asynchronously.
cues.zh: 这应该意味着奖励模型最终会非常接近人类真正想要的奖励函数。但我喜欢的一点是，整个过程是异步进行的。

cues.en: It's all going on at the same time. The agent isn't waiting for the human. It's constantly interacting with environment, getting rewards from the reward model and trying to learn at many times faster than real time. And the reward model isn't waiting either, it's continually training on all of the feedback that it's got so far. When it gets new feedback, it just adds that to the dataset and keeps on training. This means the system is actually training for tens or hundreds of seconds for each second of human time used. So the human is presented with a pair of clips and gives feedback which takes just a few seconds to do. And while that's happening, the reward model is updating to better reflect the previous feedback it got, and the agent is spending several minutes of subjective time learning and improving using that slightly improved reward model. So by the time the human is done giving feedback on those clips and it's time for the next pair, the agent has had time to improve. So the next pair of clips will have new hopefully better behavior for the human to evaluate. This means that it's able to use the humans time quite efficiently. Now to further improve that efficiency,
cues.zh: 这一切都在同时进行。智能体没有在等人类。它不断与环境交互，从奖励模型获得奖励，并试图以比实时快很多倍的速度学习。奖励模型也没有在等，它一直在用目前获得的所有反馈进行训练。当它得到新反馈时，就把它加入数据集并继续训练。这意味着，人类每花一秒，系统实际上会训练几十秒甚至几百秒。所以，人类会看到一对片段并给出反馈，这只需要几秒钟。而在这一过程中，奖励模型在更新，以更好地反映之前得到的反馈；智能体则花好几分钟的主观时间，用这个稍微改进的奖励模型来学习和提升。因此，当人类给完这些片段的反馈、该看下一对片段时，智能体已经有时间改进了。这样，下一对片段就会有新的、希望是更好的行为供人类评估。这意味着它能相当高效地利用人类的时间。现在，为了进一步提高这种效率，

cues.en: the system doesn't just choose the clips randomly,
cues.zh: 系统并不是随机选择片段，

cues.en: it tries to select clips where the reward model is uncertain about what the reward should be. Like there's no point asking for feedback if you're already pretty sure you know what the answer is. Right? So this means that the user is most likely to see clips from unusual moments when the agent has worked out something new and the reward model doesn't know what to make of it. That maximizes the value of the information provided by the human which improves the speed the system can learn. So what about the usual reinforcement learning safety problems like negative side effects and reward gaming? You might think that if you use a neural network for your reward signal, it would be very vulnerable to things like reward gaming since the reward model is just an approximation and we know that neural networks are very vulnerable to adversarial examples and so on. And it's true that if you stop updating the reward model, the agent will quickly learn to exploit it to find strategies that the reward model scores highly but the true reward doesn't.
cues.zh: 它会尽量挑选奖励模型对“奖励应该是多少”不确定的片段。就像如果你已经相当确定答案是什么，再问反馈就没意义了。对吧？所以这意味着，用户最可能看到智能体想出某些新东西、而奖励模型又不知道该怎么理解的那些不寻常时刻的片段。这能最大化人类所提供信息的价值，从而提升系统的学习速度。那么，常见的强化学习安全问题呢，比如负面副作用和奖励作弊？你可能会想，如果用神经网络作为奖励信号，它会很容易受到奖励作弊之类问题的影响，因为奖励模型只是一个近似，而且我们知道神经网络很容易受到对抗样本等影响。确实，如果你停止更新奖励模型，智能体会很快学会利用它，找到一些奖励模型给高分、但真实奖励并不高的策略。

cues.en: But the constant updating of the reward model actually provides pretty good protection against this and the way that the clips are chosen is part of that. If the agent discovers some crazy new illegitimate strategy to cheat and get high reward,
cues.zh: 但奖励模型的持续更新其实能很好地防止这种情况，而片段的选择方式也是其中一环。如果智能体发现了某种疯狂的新违规策略来作弊、拿高奖励，

cues.en: that's going to involve unusual novel behavior which will make the reward model uncertain.
cues.zh: 那必然涉及不寻常的新奇行为，奖励模型对此就会不确定。

cues.en: So the human will immediately be shown clips of the new behavior and if it's reward gaming rather than real progress, the human will give feedback saying no, that's not what I want.
cues.zh: 于是人类会立刻看到这些新行为的片段，如果这是奖励作弊而非真正的进步，人类就会给出反馈说不行，这不是我想要的。

cues.en: The reward model will update on that feedback and become more accurate and the agent will no longer be able to use that reward gaming strategy. So the idea is pretty neat and it seems to have some safety advantages. Is. How well does it actually work? Is it as effective as just programming a reward function? Well, for the backflip it seems like it definitely is and it's especially impressive when you note that this is two hours of time to write this reward function which needs a lot of expertise
cues.zh: 奖励模型会根据这些反馈更新，变得更准确，智能体也就不能再使用那种刷奖励策略了。所以这个想法相当巧妙，似乎还有一些安全优势。那它实际效果到底如何？它能像直接编写奖励函数一样有效吗？嗯，就后空翻任务来说，似乎确实如此；尤其值得注意的是，编写这个奖励函数要花两小时，而且需要大量专业知识

cues.en: compared to under one hour of rating clips which needs basically no expertise. So this is two hours of expert time versus one hour of novice time. Now they also tried it on the standard Mojoko simulated robotics tasks that have standard reward functions defined for them.
cues.zh: 相比之下，给片段打分不到一小时，而且基本不需要专业知识。所以这是两小时的专家时间对一小时的新手时间。现在他们还在标准的 MuJoCo 模拟机器人任务上做了尝试，这些任务都定义了标准奖励函数。

cues.en: Here, it tends to do not quite as well as regular reinforcement learning that's just directly given the reward function,
cues.zh: 在这种场景下，它的表现往往不如直接给定奖励函数的常规强化学习，

cues.en: but it tends to do almost as well and sometimes it even does better, which is kind of surprising. They also tried it on Atari games.
cues.zh: 但它的表现通常几乎一样好，有时甚至更好，这有点令人意外。他们还在 Atari 游戏上做了尝试。

cues.en: Now for those it needed more feedback because the task is more complex, but again it tended to do almost as well as just providing the correct reward function for several of the games. Also, there's kind of a fun implementation detail here. They had to modify the games to not show the score, Otherwise, the agent might learn to just read the score off the screen and use that. They wanted to rely on the feedback. So it seems like reward modeling is not much less effective than just providing a reward function. But the headline to me is that they were able to train these agents to do things for which they had no reward function at all, like the backflip of course. They also got the cheater robot to stand on one leg, which is a task I don't think they ever tried to write a reward function for. And in Enduro, which is an Atari game, a racing game, they managed to train the agent using reward modeling to stay level with other cars, even though the game score rewards you for going fast and overtaking them. And what all this means is that this type of method is again expanding the range of tasks machines can tackle.
cues.zh: 而对于这些任务，它需要更多反馈，因为任务更复杂；但同样，在好几款游戏里，它的表现几乎和直接提供正确奖励函数一样好。还有一个挺有趣的实现细节：他们必须修改游戏，不显示分数，否则智能体可能会学会直接从屏幕上读分数来用。他们希望智能体依赖反馈。所以看起来，奖励建模并不比直接提供奖励函数差多少。但对我来说，最重要的结论是：他们能把这些智能体训练去完成完全没有奖励函数的任务，比如后空翻。他们还让 Cheetah 机器人单腿站立，我觉得他们以前从没想过为这个任务写奖励函数。在 Atari 赛车游戏 Enduro 中，他们用奖励建模训练智能体，让它与其他车保持并驾齐驱，尽管游戏分数奖励的是开得快和超车。而这一切意味着，这类方法再次扩展了机器能处理的任务范围。

cues.en: It's not just tasks we can write programs to do or tasks we can write programs to evaluate
cues.zh: 这不仅是我们能写程序去完成的任务，也不仅是我们能写程序去评估的任务

cues.en: or even tasks we're able to do ourselves. All that's required is that it's easy to evaluate outputs that you know good results when you see them and that's a lot of tasks.
cues.zh: 甚至不只是我们自己能做的任务。所需要的只是输出容易评估——你看到好结果时能认出来——而这样的任务有很多。

cues.en: But it's not everything.
cues.zh: 但这并不是全部。

cues.en: Consider for example, a task like writing a novel.
cues.zh: 比如，考虑写小说这样的任务。

cues.en: Like sure, you can read two novels and say which one you liked more,
cues.zh: 当然，你可以读两本小说，说出自己更喜欢哪一本，

cues.en: but this system needed 900 comparisons to learn what a backflip is. Even if we assume that writing a novel is no more complicated than that,
cues.zh: 但这个系统需要 900 次比较才学会什么是后空翻。即使我们假设写小说并不比这更复杂，

cues.en: does that mean comparing 900 pairs of AI generated novels? And a lot of tasks are like this. What if we want our machine to run a company or design something complex like a city's transportation system or a computer chip. We can't write a program that does it. We can't write a program that evaluates it. We can't reliably do it ourselves enough to make a good dataset.
cues.zh: 这是否意味着要比较 900 对 AI 生成的小说？很多任务都是这样。如果我们想让机器经营一家公司，或设计像城市交通系统、计算机芯片这样复杂的东西呢？我们写不出程序来完成它。我们写不出程序来评估它。我们自己也无法可靠地做足够多次，来做出好的数据集。

cues.en: We can't even evaluate it ourselves without taking way too much time and resources.
cues.zh: 我们甚至没法自己评估它，因为会耗费太多时间和资源。

cues.en: So we're screwed, right? Not necessarily.
cues.zh: 那我们没戏了，对吧？倒也不一定。

cues.en: There are some approaches that might work for these kinds of problems and we'll talk about them in a later video.
cues.zh: 有一些方法可能能解决这类问题，我们会在之后的视频里讲。

cues.zh: 我最近意识到，我最好的解释

cues.en: and ideas tend to come from actual conversations with people. So I've been trying a thing where for each video, I first have a couple of video calls with Patreon supporters,
cues.zh: 和想法往往来自和人们的实际对话。所以我一直在尝试一件事：每期视频前，我先和 Patreon 支持者进行几次视频通话，

cues.zh: 我会试着把想法过一遍，看看大家有什么问题、哪里不清楚等等。所以我要非常感谢帮助制作这期视频的支持者们。你们知道自己是谁。我特别感谢 Jake Ehrlich。

So thank you again to all of you. If you like learning about AI safety more than you like learning about mattresses and VPNs,
cues.zh: 不，我其实拒绝了这期视频的一个赞助邀约。我承认我动心过，因为那家公司的产品我用了大概十年，而且报价有几千英镑。但他们想让我念完一整套六十秒长的广告词，我就想，算了，不想浪费大家的时间。而我也没必要这么做，因为我有 Patreon。所以再次感谢大家。如果你对了解 AI 安全比对了解床垫和 VPN 更感兴趣，
